archetype.name: Pocket Passer (accuracy-first)
archetype.definition: A 36-year-old rhythm thrower who wins by putting the ball where it belongs on short and intermediate throws from the pocket, but adds almost nothing with his legs and gives up too many sacks when the first read isn't there.

report.headline: Accurate and interception-free so far, but sacks and a thinning cast loom
report.take:
Geno Smith is doing in New York what he did at his best in Seattle: completing passes at a rate few quarterbacks match. His 72.6% completion rate ranks 4th of 42, his CPOE is +5.5, and only one charted qualifier throws a lower share of bad balls (4.3%). This isn't new. He posted CPOE near +5.6 in both 2022 and 2024 and a bottom-five bad-throw rate in three of his last four seasons. After a 2025 in Las Vegas where his EPA per play fell to -0.10 (50th of 65), +0.156 per dropback here is a real rebound, built on a skill he has shown for years.

The efficiency, though, rests on a thin and lopsided base. The 68 short throws are steady but ordinary (+0.127 EPA). The jump in value comes from 29 throws of 10+ air yards: 17 intermediate attempts at +0.51 EPA and 12 deep attempts at +2.24 per play with 3 touchdowns and a 36-point CPOE. Twelve deep balls producing three scores is not a rate anyone keeps up. His air yards to the sticks (-2.11) and 7.4-yard intended depth also show he is mostly a checkdown-and-rhythm passer, which matches his career aDOT of 6.6 to 8.0.

The numbers hide two things. First, the zero interceptions. He threw 15 in 2024 and 17 in 2025, ranking 61st and 65th, and he already has three turnover-worthy fumbles this year, so the clean sheet is luck as much as growth. Second, the sacks. A 9.3% sack rate (35th of 42) and 39% pressure-to-sack rate (30th of 32) come with a 2.94-second time to throw, his slowest on record. He isn't extending plays to create: scrambles lose EPA, and his two designed runs were both stuffed. Half his sacks (6 of 12) have come on third down, where the Jets average 9 yards to go behind a run game ranked 27th in EPA. Those long third downs set up the sacks.

The game log fits this read. He was excellent against Tennessee and Detroit, two defenses now ranked 21st and 32nd. He was fine against Green Bay (26th). He was shut down by Chicago (5th), going 8 of 15 for -4.9 EPA. The baseline is a competent, accurate starter whose output follows his protection and his opponent. That matters this week, because four offensive regulars were listed out as of Oct. 5.

strengths.title: Accuracy that holds across seasons
strengths.body: He is 4th in completion rate and 2nd-lowest in bad-throw rate, and his CPOE sits in the top ten. This is the most stable part of his profile. He posted a CPOE around +5.6 with a top-three bad-throw rate in 2022 and 2024, so expect it to last even as other numbers come back to earth.

strengths.title: Punishing defenses beyond 10 yards
strengths.body: When he gets time to push the ball, it has paid off: +0.51 EPA on intermediate throws and +2.24 on deep throws, with all three of his deep attempts that scored going for touchdowns. Some of that is real, since he places the ball well downfield. But 29 combined attempts is a small sample, and a 36-point deep CPOE will shrink sharply. Treat it as a useful trait, not a weekly engine.

concerns.title: Sacks that aren't buying anything
concerns.body: He holds the ball longer than ever (2.94s) and converts pressure into sacks at the 30th-worst rate of 32. Unlike a scrambler, he gets nothing back for it: scrambles lose EPA and designed runs are dead. His career says this is who he is, with a 46% pressure-to-sack rate in 2025 and 36% in 2024. Long third downs from a weak run game make it worse.

concerns.title: Clean ball security won't last
concerns.body: Zero interceptions through 117 attempts ranks 1st, but he led or nearly led the league in picks the last two seasons. He also already has three turnover-worthy fumbles. Expect interceptions to show up at something like his career rate, roughly one every other game or more often.

concerns.title: Supporting cast thinning out
concerns.body: Guard Dylan Parham (86% of snaps), receiver Adonai Mitchell (+0.58 EPA per target), running back Breece Hall (+0.85 EPA per target) and tight end Mason Taylor were all listed out as of Oct. 5. That would take away a starting blocker and three of his more productive outlets, leaving more of the load on Garrett Wilson and rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq. These are short-term absences, but they hit exactly the protection and quick-game options his style depends on.

trend.note: Passing EPA went 9.8, 4.3 and 10.9 against three weak defenses, then -4.9 on just 15 attempts against Chicago's 5th-ranked unit. His output has tracked opponent quality more than any steady climb or slide.

nextGame.headline: Generous QB matchup, but a sack-capable front and missing pieces
nextGame.body:
Cleveland is a mid-pack defense (16th in EPA, 13th against the pass) that has been kind to quarterbacks: 18.4 PPR and 2.25 touchdowns allowed per game, both bottom-ten. Its explosive-pass rate (21st) gives his intermediate and deep game room to work. The problem is its 9th-ranked sack rate, which goes straight at his biggest weakness. Cleveland's run defense is soft (25th in EPA, worst explosive-run rate), which could finally give the Jets manageable third downs if they can run without Hall.

Availability cuts both ways. On the Jets side, Parham, Mitchell, Hall and Taylor were all listed out as of Oct. 5, with return estimates set to game day, so their final status is the biggest variable in his outlook. If they sit, he loses a starting guard and three efficient targets. For Cleveland, defensive tackle Mason Graham (52% of snaps) is questionable with an MCL and ankle sprain; his absence would ease interior pressure. Cleveland is also without its center and a guard, which mainly hurts its own offense. That offense is the most pass-happy in the league (+7.2% pass rate over expected) and faces a Jets defense that ranks 27th against short passes, so this may not be a pure grind.

keyMatchups.title: Browns pass rush vs. sack-prone pocket
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland sacks quarterbacks at the 9th-best rate, and he goes down on nearly 4 in 10 pressures. With Parham likely out and Graham's status uncertain, the interior matchup decides whether he gets the 2.9 seconds he wants.

keyMatchups.title: Soft run defense could fix third downs
keyMatchups.body: His third downs average 9 yards to go, and that is where half his sacks have come. Cleveland allows the league's highest explosive-run rate. Even a Hall-less Jets ground game could gain enough on early downs to keep him out of obvious passing situations.

keyMatchups.title: A defense that gives up QB scoring
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland ranks 26th in touchdowns allowed to quarterbacks and 20th in yards. That fits a passer who has been at his best against non-elite defenses this year.

nextGame.watch: Whether Parham and Graham play. The interior protection matchup decides whether his accuracy gets a chance to show up or gets buried under another three-plus sacks.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy is real and should keep his completion rate around 67 to 71% with low bad-throw rates, as it has for most of four seasons. What won't hold are the zero interceptions and the deep-ball touchdown rate. His career says picks are coming, and 3 scores on 12 deep throws will cool to something far more ordinary. Efficiency should drift from +0.156 per dropback toward the +0.07 to +0.09 range of his good Seattle years. That is still a solid starter, but not a top-ten one.

The sacks are the stubborn part. They have been a problem in three of his last four seasons, and they will keep capping drives unless the Jets' 27th-ranked run game improves enough to shorten third downs. His weekly output will keep swinging with the opponent: good against bottom-half defenses, rough against good fronts. How fast his skill players return matters a lot for a passer who lives on the quick game.
swingFactors: Health of Parham, Hall, Mitchell and Taylor
Whether the run game can shorten third downs
How quickly interceptions return to his career rate

bets.reason: He ranks 30th of 32 in pressure-to-sack rate and Cleveland's sack rate ranks 9th. Starting guard Parham was listed out as of Oct. 5. The only thing working against this is Graham's questionable tag on Cleveland's line.

bets.lean: Fade the zero-interception streak; lean toward at least one pick
bets.reason: His spotless 0 interceptions run against back-to-back seasons of 15 and 17 interceptions, ranked 61st and 65th. He also has three turnover-worthy fumbles this year. Losing efficient targets like Mitchell and Hall raises the chance of forced throws.

Accuracy is his most stable trait, with a top-ten CPOE and the 2nd-lowest bad-throw rate this year, plus a long track record. Cleveland is a middle-of-the-pack defense against short throws (18th) and doesn't take away the quick game.

confidence.note: Four games, with efficiency inflated by a 12-attempt deep sample, but the core accuracy and sack traits are backed by years of career data. Final status of four injured Jets is unknown.
